slides.title: Prothrombin time and INR (PT/INR)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (sodium citrate, light-blue-top tube); at home — fingertip capillary blood  ·  Units: s

What it is used for: PT/INR is most often used to see how well warfarin (an anticoagulant blood thinner) is working — the provider may change the dose based on results; to find the reason for abnormal clots or unusual bleeding; to check clotting before a procedure or surgery that may cause bleeding; and to check for liver problems and vitamin K deficiency.
PT/INR is often done with a PTT test, which also checks for clotting problems but looks at different coagulation factors.

slides.title: Prothrombin time and INR (PT/INR)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: People taking warfarin need frequent blood tests: the INR shows how fast blood clots and helps the doctor decide whether the dose needs changing and keep the patient in a safe range. Too much medicine can cause bleeding; too little can allow a clot. Some newer direct oral anticoagulants do not need regular blood testing.

Blood thinners prevent clots from forming but do not break up existing clots. Anticoagulants such as heparin or warfarin slow the clotting process; antiplatelets such as aspirin and clopidogrel stop platelets from clumping. Regular blood tests may be needed to check clotting: enough medicine to prevent clots, but not so much that it causes bleeding.

slides.title: Prothrombin time and INR (PT/INR)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Physiology: Prothrombin is a protein made by the liver and one of the clotting (coagulation) factors, which work together to form a clot after an injury. Factor levels that are too low can cause too much bleeding; levels that are too high can cause dangerous clots in arteries or veins.

PT measures how many seconds it takes for a clot to form in a blood sample. Because results vary between labs and methods, an INR (international normalized ratio) is calculated, making results from different labs or methods easier to compare.
PT reflects primarily the clotting ability of factors I (fibrinogen), II, V, VII and X; if any of these is too low, clotting takes longer than normal.

slides.title: Prothrombin time and INR (PT/INR)
cols: On warfarin, an INR that is too high means a risk of dangerous bleeding because blood takes longer than normal to clot; the dose may be changed. Without warfarin, a high PT/INR (slow clotting) may be due to a bleeding disorder, liver disease or vitamin K deficiency.

On warfarin, an INR that is too low means a risk of dangerous clots because blood clots too easily. Without warfarin, a low PT/INR (clotting too quickly) may be due to a clotting disorder, vitamin K supplements or a diet high in vitamin K, or certain medicines.

slides.title: Prothrombin time and INR (PT/INR)
bullets: Pre-analytics: If you take warfarin, you may need to delay your daily dose until after testing — as your provider instructs.

The sample may come from a vein or a fingertip. People on long-term warfarin may be trained to test at home with a finger-prick drop, a test strip and a small device; results are reviewed with the provider.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, coagulation tests (including prothrombin time) use a sodium citrate tube (usually light-blue top): citrate removes calcium by forming calcium salts. This tube requires a full draw and gentle inversion to mix the blood with the additive.

slides.title: Prothrombin time and INR (PT/INR)
bullets: If a routine coagulation assay is the only test ordered, a single light-blue tube may be drawn; if contamination by tissue fluids or thromboplastins is a concern, a non-additive tube is drawn first. When several tubes are drawn, they are filled in a set order so additives are not carried between tubes.
WHO lists underfilling a tube, so that the anticoagulant-to-blood ratio is greater than 1:9, among the factors that increase the risk of hemolysis.

Interferences: Some medicines and supplements affect results, as can alcohol, foods high in vitamin K (such as green leafy vegetables), soybean and canola oils and high-fat diets. Ask the provider what to avoid before the test.

slides.title: Prothrombin time and INR (PT/INR)
bullets: With warfarin, high amounts of vitamin K work against the drug (other blood thinners are not affected by vitamin K), so diet should not change sharply without talking to the doctor. Aspirin-containing products, many over-the-counter medicines (pain relievers, cold and allergy medicines, ibuprofen), vitamins and herbal products can interact with blood thinners.
Limitations: To understand PT/INR results, the provider considers symptoms, history and other blood tests. Liver tests such as AST and ALT are sometimes ordered with it.

slides.title: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (sodium citrate, light-blue-top tube)  ·  Units: s

What it is used for: The test is used to find the cause of too much bruising or bleeding (for example, to help diagnose hemophilia); to monitor heparin, a medicine used to prevent and treat clots, so the dose is safe and effective; to check bleeding risk in high-risk people; and to check for clotting problems related to autoimmune diseases such as lupus and antiphospholipid syndrome.
For a fuller picture, a PT is often ordered with the PTT: it measures other clotting factors the PTT does not check, and the provider compares both results.

slides.title: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: After an injury many blood proteins — coagulation (clotting) factors, most of them made by the liver — work together to form a clot. A PTT measures how many seconds a sample takes to clot and checks how much of a specific group of clotting factors there is and how well they work.

The APTT measures the clotting ability of factors VIII, IX, XI and XII; if any is too low, clotting takes longer. So the APTT is prolonged in hemophilia A or B, while the PT is normal in most people with hemophilia.

slides.title: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
cols: If blood took longer than normal to clot (a prolonged PTT), it may be a sign of hemophilia A or B, liver disease, a lack of vitamin K, inherited disorders such as von Willebrand disease, too much heparin, certain types of leukemia, or autoimmune diseases such as lupus anticoagulant syndrome.

If blood clotted faster than normal (a short PTT), it may be a sign of the early stage of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), high clotting factor levels during inflammation, pregnancy or cancer, or advanced cancer of the ovaries, colon or pancreas.

slides.title: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, coagulation tests (including prothrombin time) use a sodium citrate tube (usually light-blue top): citrate removes calcium by forming calcium salts. This tube requires a full draw and gentle inversion to mix the blood with the additive.

If a routine coagulation assay is the only test ordered, a single light-blue tube may be drawn; if contamination by tissue fluids or thromboplastins is a concern, a non-additive tube is drawn first. When several tubes are drawn, they are filled in a set order so additives are not carried between tubes.

slides.title: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
bullets: WHO lists underfilling a tube, so that the anticoagulant-to-blood ratio is greater than 1:9, among the factors that increase the risk of hemolysis.

Interferences: Autoimmune diseases can make the PTT show slower clotting than is actually the case: test chemicals react with autoantibodies in the sample, so it clots more slowly than blood in the body. More tests are usually ordered if this is suspected.
A mixing test helps determine whether the problem is in the clotting factors or is caused by antibodies blocking them, as in autoimmune disorders or acquired hemophilia.

slides.title: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
bullets: Limitations: A sample clotting faster or slower than usual does not necessarily mean a medical condition: clotting in a test can differ from clotting in the body, so unusual results lead to more tests. If a lupus-related clotting disorder is suspected, an LA-PTT is used.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (sodium citrate, light-blue-top tube)

What it is used for: Fibrinogen is another name for clotting factor I. The fibrinogen test helps assess the ability to form a blood clot and is ordered with other clotting tests or when PT and/or APTT results are abnormal.

Fibrinogen is one of the coagulation factor tests, which check whether a factor is too high or too low, missing or not working right. They are also used to follow people with known factor problems or taking blood thinners.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Fibrinogen is a protein important for blood clot formation (coagulation). Another protein, thrombin, removes small pieces (fibrinopeptides) from it, converting fibrinogen to fibrin, the main protein in blood clots. Fibrin proteins attach to each other, forming the stable network of the clot.
After an injury, platelets form a plug; activated fibrin, a long, thin and sticky protein, forms a mesh that holds the platelet plug in place and traps red blood cells to form the clot.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
cols: Higher than normal clotting factor levels may mean a disorder that makes blood clot more than it should; factor levels can be high during inflammation, pregnancy or cancer.

Low or absent fibrinogen leads to bleeding. In congenital afibrinogenemia (about 1 in 1 million newborns) there is no fibrinogen and clots do not form: bleeding from the umbilical stump, nose, gums or tongue and into joints and muscles. In hypofibrinogenemia fibrinogen is decreased — the less there is, the more severe the bleeding.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
cols: In dysfibrinogenemia fibrinogen is present at normal levels but works abnormally, which can lead to excessive bleeding or abnormal clotting (thrombosis).

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
cols: In disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), overactive clotting comes first and then uses up platelets and clotting factors, leading to bleeding. DIC is often linked to sepsis, severe injury, burns, major surgery, pregnancy problems or cancer; several blood tests and a scoring system are used for diagnosis.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, coagulation tests (including prothrombin time) use a sodium citrate tube (usually light-blue top): citrate removes calcium by forming calcium salts. This tube requires a full draw and gentle inversion to mix the blood with the additive.

If a routine coagulation assay is the only test ordered, a single light-blue tube may be drawn; if contamination by tissue fluids or thromboplastins is a concern, a non-additive tube is drawn first. When several tubes are drawn, they are filled in a set order so additives are not carried between tubes.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
bullets: Limitations: The provider may order other tests to find the cause of a clotting factor problem. Bleeding disorders caused by other conditions usually involve low levels of two or more factors, whereas inherited ones usually involve only one.

slides.title: D-dimer
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (tube type per laboratory instructions)

What it is used for: A D-dimer test checks whether a clot may be present and whether more tests for clotting disorders are needed — deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and stroke. It is also used to monitor treatment of DIC.

DVT signs: leg pain or tenderness, swelling, redness or darkening of the skin, skin that feels warm. PE signs: trouble breathing, cough, chest pain, rapid heartbeat and breathing; many people with PE have no symptoms. Both DVT and PE need quick medical treatment.

slides.title: D-dimer
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: According to NHLBI, D-dimer tests may be used as a first step to look for signs of a clot in otherwise healthy people; high levels suggest possible DVT.

Physiology: D-dimer is a protein fragment made when a blood clot dissolves. It is not usually found in the blood unless the body is making or breaking up clots. Normally the body dissolves a clot once an injury heals; with a clotting disorder, clots can form without injury or fail to dissolve when they should.
D-dimer is released when the fibrin proteins (proteins that help stop bleeding) in a clot dissolve.

slides.title: D-dimer
cols: A high D-dimer may be a sign of a clotting disorder; more tests are needed to find the clot or the type of disorder. But high D-dimer is not always caused by clotting disorders: pregnancy, heart disease, rheumatoid arthritis, recent surgery, older age and being immobilized can also raise it.
A low or normal D-dimer means a clotting disorder is probably not present.

slides.title: D-dimer
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test.
Interferences: Blood thinners may cause a false-negative D-dimer: the test suggests no clotting disorder when one is actually present.

Limitations: If D-dimer is abnormal, imaging may be ordered to look for a clot: Doppler ultrasound (blood flow in veins), CT angiography, a ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan. CT pulmonary angiography is the main test to diagnose pulmonary embolism.

slides.title: Coagulation factors (VIII, IX, etc.)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (sodium citrate, light-blue-top tube)  ·  Units: %

What it is used for: The tests check whether one or more factors are too high or too low, missing or not working right. They are ordered after an abnormal PT/INR and/or PTT, with a family history of factor problems such as hemophilia, with conditions that affect factors (severe liver disease, lack of vitamin K, etc.) or with signs of bleeding or too much clotting, and to follow people with known factor problems or taking blood thinners.

slides.title: Coagulation factors (VIII, IX, etc.)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: To find which bleeding disorder is present: von Willebrand factor (vWF) amount and function; factor VIII activity (very low levels may mean hemophilia A; the assay also assesses severity); a Bethesda test for antibodies blocking factor VIII or IX; factor XIII antigen and activity.

Hemophilia is diagnosed with screening tests (CBC, APTT, PT, fibrinogen) followed by more specific clotting factor tests of factor VIII and IX activity, which show the type and severity and help plan treatment.

slides.title: Coagulation factors (VIII, IX, etc.)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Physiology: Coagulation factors are blood proteins that help form clots to stop bleeding after an injury; the liver makes most of them. Normally they are turned off; with bleeding, platelets become stickier and release molecules that turn on the factors, which work together in a chain reaction to form a firm clot. Each factor has a name (such as fibrinogen or prothrombin) and a Roman numeral.

slides.title: Coagulation factors (VIII, IX, etc.)
cols: Higher than normal factors may mean a disorder that makes blood clot more than it should; the provider may recommend medicine, heart-healthy lifestyle changes and avoiding estrogen-containing birth control pills or menopausal hormone therapy.

Low or missing factors may mean a bleeding disorder; depending on which factors were tested, results may show its type and severity. Inherited disorders usually involve only one factor; disorders caused by other conditions usually involve two or more.

slides.title: Coagulation factors (VIII, IX, etc.)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, coagulation tests (including prothrombin time) use a sodium citrate tube (usually light-blue top): citrate removes calcium by forming calcium salts. This tube requires a full draw and gentle inversion to mix the blood with the additive.

slides.title: Coagulation factors (VIII, IX, etc.)
bullets: If a routine coagulation assay is the only test ordered, a single light-blue tube may be drawn; if contamination by tissue fluids or thromboplastins is a concern, a non-additive tube is drawn first. When several tubes are drawn, they are filled in a set order so additives are not carried between tubes.

slides.title: Coagulation factors (VIII, IX, etc.)
bullets: Limitations: Results are reported as a percentage of a “normal” factor level: the average normal is 100%, with the normal range generally defined as 50% to 150%. Severity is based on baseline activity before treatment. The 2001 classification did not address levels of 40–50%; in 2021 ISTH recommended the terms “symptomatic carrier” and “asymptomatic carrier” for women and girls with a hemophilia gene and levels ≥ 40%.

slides.title: Coagulation factors (VIII, IX, etc.)
bullets: Umbilical cord blood testing finds low factor VIII better than low factor IX, because factor IX does not reach normal levels until a baby is at least 6 months old; a mildly low factor IX at birth does not necessarily mean hemophilia B, and a repeat test may be needed.

slides.title: Protein C and protein S
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (tube type per laboratory instructions)

What it is used for: The tests help find the cause of an unexplained clot and the risk of future clots, check for protein C or S deficiency and its type, and follow levels when the underlying condition changes. Activity (functional tests) is measured first, then, if needed, the quantity: a deficiency may come from too little protein or from protein that does not work properly.

Testing may be needed after a clot before age 50 without a known reason, a clot in an unusual location (veins of the kidneys, liver or brain), several clots, a family member with a serious inherited deficiency or a clot at a young age, or in a newborn with a clotting disorder.

slides.title: Protein C and protein S
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Proteins C and S work together to prevent blood from clotting too much. With a deficiency, blood may clot too much, even without an injury, which can cause deep vein thrombosis and life-threatening pulmonary embolism.

slides.title: Protein C and protein S
cols: Higher than normal levels of protein C or S are not known to cause any health problems.

Most protein C and S deficiencies are acquired: infections, liver or kidney disease, lack of vitamin K, cancer and chemotherapy, medicines such as birth control pills and warfarin, pregnancy and DIC. In rare cases they are inherited.

slides.title: Protein C and protein S
cols: Low levels of protein C or S, or proteins that do not work well, mean a higher risk of a blood clot; the level of risk depends on how abnormal the results are.

slides.title: Protein C and protein S
bullets: Pre-analytics: If tested because of a clot, wait until fully recovered — testing too soon gives inaccurate results. The provider may ask you not to take blood thinners for several days or longer before the test; never stop a prescription medicine without talking with the provider.

Limitations: If an inherited deficiency is suspected, a genetic test may be needed. An inherited deficiency does not mean a clot will happen, but the risk is raised for life; an acquired deficiency may be temporary or long-lasting.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: /µL, ×10⁹/L
What it is used for: A platelet count, often part of a complete blood count, is used to diagnose or monitor conditions that cause too much bleeding or clotting.

Signs of low platelets: bleeding for a long time after a minor cut, nosebleeds, unexplained bruising, pinpoint red spots (petechiae) or purple, red or brown spots (purpura), heavy or long periods, blood in urine or stool. Signs of high platelets: numbness of hands and feet, headache, dizziness, weakness, pain, swelling and warmth in the lower legs.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Platelet function tests check the platelets’ ability to form clots: closure time, viscoelastometry, aggregometry, lumiaggregometry, flow cytometry (only at certain centers) and bleeding time, which was once common but is not used much anymore. They are used in complex surgery, with a personal or family bleeding history, and in people taking blood thinners.

Physiology: Platelets are small blood cells formed in the bone marrow and are essential for blood clotting. When you get hurt, platelets, proteins and cells stick together into a clot that stops the bleeding.
The spleen normally stores about one-third of the body’s platelets; an enlarged spleen may remove or store too many.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 1/3
bullets: High: Thrombocytosis (a high count) can make blood clot more than needed, and clots can block blood flow. Causes include certain cancers such as lung or breast cancer, anemia, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis), rheumatoid arthritis, a viral or bacterial infection and severe blood loss.

High: A high platelet count not caused by another condition is thrombocythemia (primary or essential); one caused by another disease or condition is thrombocytosis (secondary or reactive), which is more common.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 2/3
bullets: Low: Thrombocytopenia (a low count) can cause too much bleeding after an injury. Causes include blood cancers such as leukemia or lymphoma; viral infections such as mononucleosis, hepatitis or measles; autoimmune disease; bone marrow infection or damage; cirrhosis; and vitamin B12 deficiency. Mild gestational thrombocytopenia can occur in pregnancy; it is not known to harm mother or fetus and usually resolves on its own.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 3/3
bullets: Low: Heparin, a medicine used to prevent clots, can through an immune reaction cause both clots and thrombocytopenia (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia). Toxic chemicals such as pesticides, arsenic and benzene, and alcohol, can damage the bone marrow and lower platelet production; some medicines can too.

Low: NHLBI defines a low platelet count as less than 150,000/µL: 100,000–150,000/µL is mild and less than 20,000/µL severe; a high count is more than 450,000/µL. The full classification is in the “Decision limits” block.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a platelet count. Before a platelet function test, medicines such as aspirin and ibuprofen may need to be stopped — only as the provider instructs.

With skin punctures the hematology specimen is collected first to minimize the effects of platelet clumping; the venepuncture order is the reverse. If more than two specimens are needed, venepuncture may give more accurate results.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

Limitations: Platelet tests are often done with an MPV (platelet size), PTT and PT/INR. In people taking anti-platelet medicine such as aspirin, platelet function results show how well the medicine is working.
Mild thrombocytopenia often has no symptoms and is often found on a routine blood test.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: A complete blood count is only one tool: for a diagnosis the provider considers medical history, symptoms and other factors, and more tests may be needed.

slides.title: Bleeding and clotting disorder work-up
bullets: Screening tests (complete blood count with platelets, PT, PTT) show whether the problem lies with platelets or clotting factors; then specific factor tests and other causes (liver disease, autoimmune conditions) are checked.

slides.title: Bleeding and clotting disorder work-up
rows: A low platelet count may point to a platelet disorder rather than a clotting factor disorder.
An abnormal PT may indicate a problem with one group of clotting factors.
An abnormal PTT may indicate a problem with another group of clotting factors.

slides.title: Bleeding and clotting disorder work-up
rows: Tells a factor deficiency apart from antibodies blocking clotting factors (autoimmune disorders, acquired hemophilia).
The amount and function of von Willebrand factor — to identify the type of von Willebrand disease.
Very low factor VIII may indicate hemophilia A and shows how severe the deficiency is.

slides.title: Bleeding and clotting disorder work-up
rows: Liver damage may be the cause of the bleeding disorder.
Detects antibodies that may signal an autoimmune condition affecting clotting.

slides.title: Bleeding and clotting disorder work-up
rows: A platelet disorder is more likely than a clotting factor disorder.
A problem with a group of clotting factors is possible; a mixing study tells deficiency from antibodies.
Antibodies blocking factor VIII or IX are likely.

slides.title: Deep vein thrombosis / pulmonary embolism (suspected)
bullets: Tests are chosen based on history and risk factors: blood tests and imaging. The main test for pulmonary embolism is CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA).

slides.title: Deep vein thrombosis / pulmonary embolism (suspected)
rows: Released when fibrin, a clotting protein, breaks down; may be a first step in otherwise healthy people.
Low blood oxygen can be a sign of a blood clot.

slides.title: Deep vein thrombosis / pulmonary embolism (suspected)
rows: A clot (clotting disorder) is unlikely; blood thinners can cause a false negative.
A clot is possible but not certain — imaging (Doppler ultrasound, CT angiography, V/Q scan) finds its location.

slides.title: Deep vein thrombosis / pulmonary embolism (suspected)
bullets: Pregnancy, heart disease, rheumatoid arthritis, recent surgery, older age and immobility can also raise D-dimer.

slides.title: The platelet count is 15 ×10⁹/L (15,000/µL). Which category is this per NHLBI?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: below 20 ×10⁹/L (20,000/µL) is severe.

Basis: < 150 ×10⁹/L (150,000/µL) is low; 100–150 ×10⁹/L (100,000–150,000/µL) mild; < 20 ×10⁹/L (20,000/µL) severe.

slides.title: Why is the hematology specimen collected first in skin puncture (WHO)?
options: Because venepuncture uses the same order
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: This order minimizes the effects of platelet clumping.

slides.title: Why is an INR calculated from the PT?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: PT varies by lab and method; the INR makes results easier to compare.

slides.title: A patient on warfarin has a very high INR. What does it mean per the source?
options: Warfarin is not working at all
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the dose may be changed.

Basis: High INR — risk of dangerous bleeding; low INR — risk of clots.

slides.title: Per CDC, which clotting factors does the APTT reflect?
options: I, II, V, VII and X
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: APTT — VIII, IX, XI, XII; PT — mainly I, II, V, VII, X.

slides.title: What do screening tests usually show in hemophilia A (CDC)?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: APTT is prolonged, PT normal in most; the CBC may also be normal.

slides.title: Modern concept of hemostasis. The hemostatic system in the norm?
bullets: 1. Hemostasis is the balance of the systems that stop bleeding and keep blood fluid: the vessel wall (endothelium), platelets, coagulation factors, anticoagulants and fibrinolysis.

2. Primary (vascular-platelet) hemostasis: vasoconstriction, adhesion of platelets to the subendothelium via vWF (GPIb), activation (release of ADP, thromboxane A2) and aggregation via fibrinogen (GPIIb/IIIa) – the platelet plug.

slides.title: Modern concept of hemostasis. The hemostatic system in the norm?
bullets: 3. Secondary (coagulation) hemostasis – the modern cell-based model: initiation (the tissue factor–VIIa complex generates a small amount of thrombin), amplification (thrombin activates platelets and factors V, VIII, XI), propagation (a lot of thrombin on the surface of the activated platelet) → fibrin, stabilized by XIIIa.

4. Natural anticoagulants: antithrombin (neutralizes IIa, Xa, IXa; heparin potentiates it), the protein C/protein S system (inactivates Va and VIIIa; activated with thrombomodulin), TFPI (inhibits TF–VIIa/Xa).

slides.title: Modern concept of hemostasis. The hemostatic system in the norm?
bullets: 5. Fibrinolysis: tPA and urokinase convert plasminogen to plasmin, plasmin degrades fibrin (D-dimer is formed); PAI-1 and α2-antiplasmin limit it.
6. The classical "cascade" (extrinsic and intrinsic pathway) is retained to explain laboratory tests: PT – extrinsic and common pathway, aPTT – intrinsic and common pathway.

slides.title: Disorders of the hemostatic system. Hypo- and hypercoagulation. DIC?
bullets: 1. Causes of hypocoagulation (bleeding): thrombocytopenia and platelet function disorders, von Willebrand disease, hemophilias (VIII, IX), vitamin K deficiency and warfarin, liver diseases, DIC, anticoagulants.

2. Hypercoagulation/thrombophilia: inherited (antithrombin, protein C/S deficiency, factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation) and acquired (antiphospholipid syndrome, tumors, pregnancy, estrogens, immobilization, surgery).

slides.title: Disorders of the hemostatic system. Hypo- and hypercoagulation. DIC?
bullets: 3. DIC is systemic activation of coagulation (sepsis, trauma, obstetric complications, tumors, APL): microthrombi and bleeding due to consumption of factors/platelets; stages – hypercoagulation, transition, hypocoagulation (consumption coagulopathy).

4. Laboratory signs of DIC: falling platelets (over time), sharp rise of D-dimer/fibrin markers, prolonged PT, decreased fibrinogen, schistocytes on the smear; overt DIC by the ISTH score ≥5 (platelets, fibrin marker, PT, fibrinogen).

slides.title: Disorders of the hemostatic system. Hypo- and hypercoagulation. DIC?
bullets: 5. Screening tests: platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen (Clauss), thrombin time, D-dimer; if needed factor activities, mixing test, vWF, lupus anticoagulant.

slides.title: Methods of examining hemostasis?
bullets: 1. Primary hemostasis: platelet count, smear (morphology, clumps), platelet function – light transmission aggregometry (gold standard), PFA-100/200; vWF antigen and activity; bleeding time – insensitive, abolished in many places.
2. Coagulation screening: PT (extrinsic and common pathway; reported as INR), aPTT (intrinsic and common pathway), fibrinogen (Clauss method), thrombin time.
3. Clarifying tests: activity of individual factors (VIII, IX, XI, etc.), mixing test (deficiency or inhibitor), lupus anticoagulant, factor XIII.

slides.title: Methods of examining hemostasis?
bullets: 4. Tests for anticoagulants and thrombophilia: antithrombin, protein C, protein S, activated protein C resistance, genetic tests (factor V Leiden, prothrombin).
5. Fibrinolysis: D-dimer (excluding VTE, DIC), fibrinogen and fibrin degradation products; global tests – thromboelastography/thromboelastometry, thrombin generation assay.
6. Correct preanalytics (3.2% citrate, 9:1, room temperature) is mandatory for all tests.
